title: Scenes 4–7: Crises, Conflict and Revelation
description: Del moves to Mai's, Del's pregnancy, Viv's exam rebellion, and Brod's revelation about the abusive father.
content_html:
The Crises Converge

In Scenes 4–7, the tensions established in the opening scenes crack open into genuine crisis. Three parallel developments drive this section: Del deepens her relationship with Mai and eventually moves into her Deptford bedsit; Del's pregnancy becomes apparent; and Viv, the apparently conformist daughter, begins to rebel in her own way — walking out of one of her A-level exams. Pinnock uses these parallel crises to show that Enid's strategy of assimilation cannot contain the complexity of her daughters' lives, and that both sisters ultimately reject the identity their mother has tried to impose on them — just in different ways.

Key Fact

Del's pregnancy belongs to Del, the elder daughter (18) — not to Viv. Enid's worry about Del in Scene 1, when she first visits Mai, is later confirmed: Del is indeed pregnant, the father absent. This is one of the play's major plot developments. Viv's parallel crisis is entirely different — it is educational and intellectual, not physical.

Del and Mai

Del's relationship with Mai intensifies across these scenes. Initially Enid brought Del to Mai hoping Mai might help control her — but Del becomes Mai's ally and eventual successor instead. Del discovers she is dyslexic, which reframes her difficulties at school: she was not lazy or rebellious in failing to engage with formal education — she was struggling with a barrier that the school system never identified. Del moves out of Enid's home and into Mai's bedsit, a decision that causes Enid enormous distress. But Mai recognises Del's potential as a healer and spiritual practitioner, and begins to train her.

Del becomes pregnant during this section of the play. The father is absent. This development confirms Enid's original fear from Scene 1 and places Del in a position of vulnerability at exactly the moment she is finding her own path through Mai. Pinnock does not present the pregnancy as a catastrophe — it is one of several things Del must navigate as she builds an identity independent of both Enid's expectations and conventional English society.

Viv's Rebellion

Viv's crisis is very different from Del's — it takes place in her head and in the exam hall rather than in the streets or at Mai's bedsit. In Scene 5, Viv walks out of one of her A-level exams. This reflects a growing crisis of identity that Viv has been suppressing alongside her studies. Viv's complaint is that the education system does not reflect her experience or heritage. She feels invisible within it — a student whose culture is absent from the curriculum she is being tested on.

Key Fact

Viv's rebellion is intellectual and cultural, not romantic or physical. After walking out of the exam, she determines to study Black Studies at university — a subject that actually includes her experience. She says something close to: no matter how hard I search for myself in these books, I am never there. This is not a rejection of education — it is a rejection of a Eurocentric education that treats her heritage as invisible.

Scene 7: Brod Tells Del the Truth

Scene 7, set at Mai's bedsit, contains one of the play's most important revelations. Brod — Enid's Windrush-generation friend — tells Del the truth about her father. Enid's husband was abusive. He subjected Enid to domestic violence. The racism he suffered at work — described by Brod as relentless and dehumanising — made him hard and cruel, turning him into someone who took out his degradation on the person closest to him. Enid eventually left him, but she never told her daughters the truth about why.

This revelation is crucial for understanding Enid's character. Her fierce protectiveness and controlling behaviour are not simply about cultural ambition — they come from a woman who survived abuse and displacement and is determined that her daughters will not experience the same. The revelation also illuminates Brod's disillusionment: he describes a friend — Gullyman — who achieved financial success but still suffered a breakdown. England's racism, Pinnock suggests, spares no one.

By Scene 6, Enid herself comes to Mai's bedsit — searching for Del, but also, Pinnock suggests, beginning to seek healing she cannot articulate. Mai reads Enid's palm and tells her she will make a long journey. This prediction introduces the possibility of reconciliation that the final scene will deliver. Mai is physically declining throughout these scenes — clearly dying — but she uses what life remains to ensure Del is ready to inherit her role.

practice_questions.text: How does Pinnock present Viv's rejection of the education system in Leave Taking? [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Perceptive analysis of Viv's rebellion as intellectual and cultural. Discusses: walking out of the exam, the complaint that the curriculum excludes her experience, her choice of Black Studies. Links to identity, belonging and the invisibility of Caribbean culture in English education.

Mid band (9–16): Clear analysis with evidence.

Lower band (1–8): Describes Viv's actions without analysing their significance.

practice_questions.text: How does Pinnock use Brod's revelation in Scene 7 to develop the audience's understanding of Enid? [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Analyses the function of Brod's revelation about Enid's abusive marriage — recontextualising her controlling behaviour from snobbery to survival. Examines Brod's dramatic function. Links to suppressed history.

Mid band (9–16): Clear analysis.

Lower band (1–8): Basic description.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Pinnock and the writer of the unseen text present a character whose behaviour is explained by hidden trauma. Consider language, form and structure. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Perceptive comparison. Analyses Pinnock's Enid — her controlling behaviour reframed by the revelation of the abusive marriage and her mother's death. Compares methods with the unseen writer.

Mid band (9–16): Clear comparison.

Lower band (1–8): Limited comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Pinnock presents Del's development as a character across the middle section of Leave Taking. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Traces Del's arc — moving to Mai's, her pregnancy, the dyslexia discovery, her emerging role as Mai's successor. Analyses Pinnock's methods. Links to cultural belonging and alternative forms of knowledge.

Mid band (9–16): Clear analysis.

Lower band (1–8): Basic description.

practice_questions.text: How does Pinnock present the impact of racism on the Windrush generation through the character of Brod? [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Analyses Brod as voice of Windrush disillusionment. Discusses his drinking, estrangement from his children, account of Enid's husband's abuse rooted in workplace racism, and Gullyman. Links to Pinnock's argument about systemic racism's long-term human cost.

Mid band (9–16): Clear analysis.

Lower band (1–8): Basic description.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Pinnock and the writer of the unseen text present two characters with contrasting personalities. Consider language, form and structure. [20 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (17–20): Perceptive comparison. Analyses Pinnock's Del and Viv — elder and younger, 18 and 17, rebellious and conformist but both ultimately rejecting Enid's assimilation. Compares with the unseen text.

Mid band (9–16): Clear comparison.

Lower band (1–8): Limited comparison.

knowledge_checks.q: Which daughter becomes pregnant in Leave Taking?
What does Viv do in Scene 5 as an act of rebellion?
options: She argues with Enid about Jamaica
She walks out of one of her A-level exams

knowledge_checks.q: In Scene 7, Brod tells Del that her father was _____ towards Enid.
Viv plans to study _____ at university — a subject that includes her Caribbean heritage.
Match each character to their crisis in Scenes 4–7:
right: Moves to Mai's bedsit; becomes pregnant; begins Obeah training
Walks out of A-level exam; plans to study Black Studies
Searches for Del at Mai's; grief after her mother's death drives emotional collapse

flashcard_questions.q: Which daughter is pregnant in Leave Taking, and why does this matter dramatically?
flashcard_questions.a: Del (the elder daughter, 18) — it confirms Enid's original fear from Scene 1, happening while Del is building an independent life at Mai's.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Viv walk out of her A-level exam?
flashcard_questions.a: She feels the Eurocentric curriculum has no place for her — 'no matter how hard I search for myself in them books, I'm never there.'

flashcard_questions.q: What does Viv plan to study at university?
flashcard_questions.a: Black Studies — a subject that reflects her Caribbean heritage and experience.

flashcard_questions.q: What truth does Brod reveal to Del in Scene 7?
flashcard_questions.a: That Del's father was abusive towards Enid — his cruelty was partly rooted in the racism he suffered at work.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the revelation about Enid's marriage reframe her character?
flashcard_questions.a: Her controlling behaviour is recontextualised as a survivor's response — driven by determination to protect her daughters, not cold ambition.

flashcard_questions.q: What disability does Del discover she has?
flashcard_questions.a: Dyslexia — explaining her struggles with formal education that the school system never identified.

flashcard_questions.q: Where does Del go to live in Scenes 4–7, and what does she do there?
flashcard_questions.a: She moves into Mai's Deptford bedsit and begins training as Mai's spiritual successor.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Mai predict when she reads Enid's palm in Scene 6?
flashcard_questions.a: That Enid will make a long journey — foreshadowing the reconciliation and spiritual reconnection to come.

flashcard_questions.q: Who is Gullyman, and why does Brod mention him?
flashcard_questions.a: A friend who achieved financial success but still suffered a breakdown — used to argue that England's racism spares no one.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the dramatic function of Brod in Scenes 2, 3 and 7?
flashcard_questions.a: The play's outsider who holds truths the family cannot tell itself — he provides the male Windrush perspective and the revelation about Enid's abusive marriage.

glossary_terms.definition: A learning difference that affects reading and writing — Del's diagnosis reframes her school struggles as unrecognised difficulty.
A sense of who one is, especially in relation to culture, heritage and the wider world.
Involving repeated cruel or violent behaviour — Enid's husband subjected her to domestic violence, a truth Brod reveals in Scene 7.
A character or event that triggers significant change — Mai acts as a catalyst for Del's development and Enid's eventual reconnection.
The loss of hope or ideals — Brod embodies the Windrush generation's disillusionment with life in Britain.
A structural technique where two storylines mirror each other — Del's and Viv's contrasting crises run in parallel across these scenes.

exam_tip_html: When writing about Scenes 4–7: Crises, Conflict and Revelation, focus your analysis on the specific dramatic and structural choices the playwright makes. Examiners reward responses that connect language details to wider themes, and that show understanding of the social and historical context in which the play was written. Avoid retelling the plot — instead, explain the effect of specific techniques on the audience.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • This lesson has covered the key ideas and dramatic techniques relevant to Scenes 4–7: Crises, Conflict and Revelation. Make sure you can discuss specific examples from the text, link techniques to themes, and embed relevant context in your analysis.
